lesson.title: Same Shape, Different Address: How Mean and Standard Deviation Steer the Bell Curve
lesson.summary: Every normal distribution is controlled by exactly two parameters, the mean and the standard deviation, which together determine the curve's location and width while every normal curve keeps the same underlying bell shape.
lesson.body:
A parameter, in statistics, is a number that describes an entire population or an entire theoretical model, as opposed to a statistic, which describes a sample. The normal distribution is called a two-parameter family of curves because exactly two numbers, the population mean, written with the Greek letter mu, and the population standard deviation, written with the Greek letter sigma, are enough to pin down one specific normal curve out of infinitely many possible ones. Once mu and sigma are known, the entire curve, every detail of its shape and position, is completely determined.

The mean, mu, controls location. It marks the exact center of the curve, the point directly under the peak, and shifting mu slides the whole bell shape left or right along the number line without changing its width or height in any way. The standard deviation, sigma, controls spread. A larger sigma stretches the curve horizontally, spreading the data over a wider range of values and lowering the peak so that the total area under the curve still equals one, while a smaller sigma compresses the curve into a taller, narrower shape clustered tightly around the mean. Critically, changing sigma never changes where the center is, and changing mu never changes how wide the curve is: the two parameters act independently.

Consider resting heart rates. In a general adult population, resting heart rate is approximately normal with a mean of 72 beats per minute and a standard deviation of 8 beats per minute. Among highly trained endurance athletes, resting heart rate is also approximately normal, but with a mean closer to 58 beats per minute and a standard deviation closer to 5 beats per minute. Both populations follow the same family of bell-shaped curve, but the athlete's curve sits farther to the left, since 58 is well below 72, and it is also narrower, since 5 is smaller than 8, reflecting heart rates that are both lower on average and more tightly clustered around that lower average. Sketching the two curves on the same axis would show two overlapping bells, one shorter and wider centered near 72, the other taller and narrower centered near 58.

This same idea explains why two different standardized tests, say one scored on a scale with mean 500 and standard deviation 100, and another scored on a scale with mean 21 and standard deviation 5, can both be modeled as normal distributions despite using completely different numbers. The shape of the underlying bell curve is identical in a mathematical sense; only its parameters, its address on the number line and its width, differ. That insight, that all normal curves are really the same shape wearing different parameters, is exactly what makes it possible to compare values from different normal distributions on a common scale, which is the idea explored next through standardization.
